reference_research_study_list.title: Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks
reference_research_study_list.abstract:
The ability to learn tasks in a sequential fashion is crucial to the
development of artificial intelligence. Neural networks are not, in general,
capable of this and it has been widely thought that catastrophic forgetting is
an inevitable feature of connectionist models. We show that it is possible to
overcome this limitation and train networks that can maintain expertise on
tasks which they have not experienced for a long time. Our approach remembers
old tasks by selectively slowing down learning on the weights important for
those tasks. We demonstrate our approach is scalable and effective by solving a
set of classification tasks based on the MNIST hand written digit dataset and
by learning several Atari 2600 games sequentially.
reference_research_study_list.full_text: Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks James Kirkpatricka, Razvan Pascanua, Neil Rabinowitza, Joel Venessa, Guillaume Desjardinsa, Andrei A. Rusua, Kieran Milana, John Quana, Tiago Ramalhoa, Agnieszka Grabska-Barwinska a, Demis Hassabisa, Claudia Clopathb, Dharshan Kumarana, and Raia Hadsella aDeepMind, London, N1C 4AG, United Kingdom bBioengineering department, Imperial College London, SW7 2AZ, London, United Kingdom Abstract The ability to learn tasks in a sequential fashion is crucial to the development of artiﬁcial intelligence. Neural networks are not, in general, capable of this and it has been widely thought that catastrophic forgetting is an inevitable feature of connectionist models. We show that it is possible to overcome this limitation and train networks that can maintain expertise on tasks which they have not experienced for a long time. Our approach remembers old tasks by selectively slowing down learning on the weights important for those tasks. We demonstrate our approach is scalable and effective by solving a set of classiﬁcation tasks based on the MNIST hand written digit dataset and by learning several Atari 2600 games sequentially. 1 Introduction Achieving artiﬁcial general intelligence requires that agents are able to learn and remember many different tasks Legg and Hutter [2007]. This is particularly difﬁcult in real-world settings: the sequence of tasks may not be explicitly labelled, tasks may switch unpredictably, and any individual task may not recur for long time intervals. Critically, therefore, intelligent agents must demonstrate a capacity for continual learning: that is, the ability to learn consecutive tasks without forgetting how to perform previously trained tasks. Continual learning poses particular challenges for artiﬁcial neural networks due to the tendency for knowledge of previously learnt task(s) (e.g. task A) to be abruptly lost as information relevant to the current task (e.g. task B) is incorporated. This phenomenon, termed catastrophic forgetting [French, 1999, McCloskey and Cohen, 1989, McClelland et al., 1995, Ratcliff, 1990], occurs speciﬁcally when the network is trained sequentially on multiple tasks because the weights in the network that are important for task A are changed to meet the objectives of task B. Whilst recent advances in machine learning and in particular deep neural networks have resulted in impressive gains in performance across a variety of domains (e.g. [Krizhevsky et al., 2012, LeCun et al., 2015]), little progress has been made in achieving continual learning. Current approaches have typically ensured that data from all tasks are simultaneously available during training. By interleaving data from multiple tasks during learning, forgetting does not occur because the weights of the network can be jointly optimized for performance on all tasks. In this regime—often referred to as the multitask learning paradigm—deep learning techniques have been used to train single agents that can successfully play multiple Atari games [Rusu et al., 2015, Parisotto et al., 2015]. If tasks are presented sequentially, multitask learning can only be used if the data are recorded by an episodic memory system and replayed to the network during training. This approach (often called system-level consolidation [McClelland et al., 1995]), is impractical for learning large numbers of tasks, as in our setting it would require the amount of memories being stored and replayed to be proportional to the number of tasks. The lack of algorithms arXiv:1612.00796v2  [cs.LG]  25 Jan 2017to support continual learning thus remains a key barrier to the development of artiﬁcial general intelligence. In marked contrast to artiﬁcial neural networks, humans and other animals appear to be able to learn in a continual fashion [Cichon and Gan, 2015]. Recent evidence suggests that the mammalian brain may avoid catastrophic forgetting by protecting previously-acquired knowledge in neocortical circuits [Cichon and Gan, 2015, Hayashi-Takagi et al., 2015, Yang et al., 2009, 2014]. When a mouse acquires a new skill, a proportion of excitatory synapses are strengthened; this manifests as an increase in the volume of individual dendritic spines of neurons [Yang et al., 2009]. Critically, these enlarged dendritic spines persist despite the subsequent learning of other tasks, accounting for retention of performance several months later [Yang et al., 2009]. When these spines are selectively “erased”, the corresponding skill is forgotten [Hayashi-Takagi et al., 2015, Cichon and Gan, 2015]. This provides causal evidence that neural mechanisms supporting the protection of these strengthened synapses are critical to retention of task performance. Together, these experimental ﬁndings—together with neurobiological models [Fusi et al., 2005, Benna and Fusi, 2016]—suggest that continual learning in the mammalian neocortex relies on a process of task-speciﬁc synaptic consolidation, whereby knowledge about how to perform a previously acquired task is durably encoded in a proportion of synapses that are rendered less plastic and therefore stable over long timescales. In this work, we demonstrate that task-speciﬁc synaptic consolidation offers a novel solution to the continual learning problem for artiﬁcial intelligence. We develop an algorithm analogous to synaptic consolidation for artiﬁcial neural networks, which we refer to as elastic weight consolidation (EWC for short). This algorithm slows down learning on certain weights based on how important they are to previously seen tasks. We show how EWC can be used in supervised learning and reinforcement learning problems to train several tasks sequentially without forgetting older ones, in marked contrast to previous deep-learning techniques. 2 Elastic weight consolidation In brains, synaptic consolidation enables continual learning by reducing the plasticity of synapses that are vital to previously learned tasks. We implement an algorithm that performs a similar operation in artiﬁcial neural networks by constraining important parameters to stay close to their old values. In this section we explain why we expect to ﬁnd a solution to a new task in the neighbourhood of an older one, how we implement the constraint, and ﬁnally how we determine which parameters are important. A deep neural network consists of multiple layers of linear projection followed by element-wise non-linearities. Learning a task consists of adjusting the set of weights and biases θof the linear projections, to optimize performance. Many conﬁgurations of θwill result in the same performance [Nielsen, 1989, Sussmann, 1992]; this is relevant for EWC: over-parameterization makes it likely that there is a solution for task B, θ∗ B, that is close to the previously found solution for task A, θ∗ A. While learning task B, EWC therefore protects the performance in task A by constraining the parameters to stay in a region of low error for task A centered around θ∗ A, as shown schematically in Figure 1. This constraint is implemented as a quadratic penalty, and can therefore be imagined as a spring anchoring the parameters to the previous solution, hence the name elastic. Importantly, the stiffness of this spring should not be the same for all parameters; rather, it should be greater for those parameters that matter most to the performance during task A. In order to justify this choice of constraint and to deﬁne which weights are most important for a task, it is useful to consider neural network training from a probabilistic perspective. From this point of view, optimizing the parameters is tantamount to ﬁnding their most probable values given some data D. We can compute this conditional probability p(θ|D) from the prior probability of the parameters p(θ) and the probability of the data p(D|θ) by using Bayes’ rule: log p(θ|D) = log p(D|θ) + logp(θ) −log p(D) (1) Note that the log probability of the data given the parameters log p(D|θ) is simply the negative of the loss function for the problem at hand −L(θ). Assume that the data is split into two independent parts, one deﬁning task A (DA) and the other task B (DB). Then, we can re-arrange equation 1: log p(θ|D) = log p(DB|θ) + logp(θ|DA) −log p(DB) (2) Note that the left hand side is still describing the posterior probability of the parameters given the entire dataset, while the right hand side only depends on the loss function for task B log p(DB|θ). 2Figure 1: elastic weight consolidation (EWC) ensures task A is remembered whilst training on task B. Training trajectories are illustrated in a schematic parameter space, with parameter regions leading to good performance on task A (gray) and on task B (cream). After learning the ﬁrst task, the parameters are at θ∗ A. If we take gradient steps according to task B alone (blue arrow), we will minimize the loss of task B but destroy what we have learnt for task A. On the other hand, if we constrain each weight with the same coefﬁcient (green arrow) the restriction imposed is too severe and we can only remember task A at the expense of not learning task B. EWC, conversely, ﬁnds a solution for task B without incurring a signiﬁcant loss on task A (red arrow) by explicitly computing how important weights are for task A. All the information about task A must therefore have been absorbed into the posterior distribution p(θ|DA). This posterior probability must contain information about which parameters were important to task Aand is therefore the key to implementing EWC. The true posterior probability is intractable, so, following the work on the Laplace approximation by Mackay [MacKay, 1992], we approximate the posterior as a Gaussian distribution with mean given by the parametersθ∗ A and a diagonal precision given by the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix F. F has three key properties [Pascanu and Bengio, 2013]: (a) it is equivalent to the second derivative of the loss near a minimum, (b) it can be computed from ﬁrst-order derivatives alone and is thus easy to calculate even for large models, and (c) it is guaranteed to be positive semi-deﬁnite. Note that this approach is similar to expectation propagation where each subtask is seen as a factor of the posterior [Eskin et al., 2004]. Given this approximation, the function Lthat we minimize in EWC is: L(θ) = LB(θ) + ∑ i λ 2 Fi(θi −θ∗ A,i)2 (3) where LB(θ) is the loss for task B only, λsets how important the old task is compared to the new one and ilabels each parameter. When moving to a third task, task C, EWC will try to keep the network parameters close to the learned parameters of both task A and B. This can be enforced either with two separate penalties, or as one by noting that the sum of two quadratic penalties is itself a quadratic penalty. 2.1 EWC allows continual learning in a supervised learning context We start by addressing the problem of whether elastic weight consolidation could allow deep neural networks to learn a set of complex tasks without catastrophic forgetting. In particular, we trained a fully connected multilayer neural network on several supervised learning tasks in sequence. Within each task, we trained the neural network in the traditional way, namely by shufﬂing the data and processing it in small batches. After a ﬁxed amount of training on each task, however, we allowed no further training on that task’s dataset. We constructed the set of tasks from the problem of classifying hand written digits from the MNIST [LeCun et al., 1998] dataset, according to a scheme previously used in the continual learning literature [Srivastava et al., 2013, Goodfellow et al., 2014]. For each task, we generated a ﬁxed, random permutation by which the input pixels of all images would be shufﬂed. Each task was thus of equal difﬁculty to the original MNIST problem, though a different solution would be required for each. Detailed description of the settings used can be found in Appendix 4.1. Training on this sequence of tasks with plain stochastic gradient descent (SGD) incurs catastrophic forgetting, as demonstrated in Figure 2A. The blue curves show performance on the testing sets of two different tasks. At the point at which the training regime switches from training on the ﬁrst task (A) to training on the second (B), the performance for task B falls rapidly, while for task A it climbs steeply. The forgetting of task A compounds further with more training time, and the addition 3Figure 2: Results on the permuted MNIST task. This problem cannot be countered by regularizing the network with a ﬁxed quadratic constraint for each weight (green curves, L2 regularization): here, the performance in task A degrades much less severely, but task B cannot be learned properly as the constraint protects all weights equally, leaving little spare capacity for learning on B. However, when we use EWC, and thus take into account how important each weight is to task A, the network can learn task B well without forgetting task A (red curves). This is exactly the expected behaviour described diagrammatically in Figure 1. Previous attempts to solve the continual learning problem for deep neural networks have relied upon careful choice of network hyperparameters, together with other standard regularization methods, in order to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. However, on this task, they have only achieved reasonable results on up to two random permutations [Srivastava et al., 2013, Goodfellow et al., 2014]. Using a similar cross-validated hyperparameter search as [Goodfellow et al., 2014], we compared traditional dropout regularization to EWC. We ﬁnd that stochastic gradient descent with dropout regularization alone is limited, and that it does not scale to more tasks (Figure 2B). In contrast, EWC allows a large number of tasks to be learned in sequence, with only modest growth in the error rates. Given that EWC allows the network to effectively squeeze in more functionality into a network with ﬁxed capacity, we might ask whether it allocates completely separate parts of the network for each task, or whether capacity is used in a more efﬁcient fashion by sharing representation. To assess this, we determined whether each task depends on the same sets of weights, by measuring the overlap between pairs of tasks’ respective Fisher information matrices (see Appendix 4.3). A small overlap means that the two tasks depend on different sets of weights (i.e. EWC subdivides the network’s weights for different tasks); a large overlap indicates that weights are being used for both the two tasks (i.e. EWC enables sharing of representations). Figure 2C shows the overlap as a function of depth. As a simple control, when a network is trained on two tasks which are very similar to each other (two versions of MNIST where only a few pixels are permutated), the tasks depend on similar sets of weights throughout the whole network (grey curve). When then the two tasks are more dissimilar from each other, the network begins to allocate separate capacity (i.e. weights) for the two tasks (black line). Nevertheless, even for the large permutations, the layers of the network closer to the output are indeed being reused for both tasks. This reﬂects the fact that the permutations make the input domain very different, but the output domain (i.e. the class labels) is shared. 2.2 EWC allows continual learning in a reinforcement learning context We next tested whether elastic weight consolidation could support continual learning in the far more demanding reinforcement learning (RL) domain. In RL, agents dynamically interact with the environment in order to develop a policy that maximizes cumulative future reward. We asked whether Deep Q Networks (DQNs)—an architecture that has achieved impressive successes in such challenging RL settings [Mnih et al., 2015]—could be harnessed with EWC to successfully support continual learning in the classic Atari 2600 task set [Bellemare et al., 2013]. Speciﬁcally, each 4experiment consisted of ten games chosen randomly from those that are played at human level or above by DQN. At training time, the agent was exposed to experiences from each game for extended periods of time. The order of presentation of the games was randomized and allowed for returning to the same games several times. At regular intervals we would also test the agent’s score on each of the ten games, without allowing the agent to train on them (Figure 3A). Notably, previous reinforcement learning approaches to continual learning have either relied on either adding capacity to the network [Ring, 1998, Rusu et al., 2016] or on learning each task in separate networks, which are then used to train a single network that can play all games[Rusu et al., 2015, Parisotto et al., 2015]. In contrast, the EWC approach presented here makes use of a single network with ﬁxed resources (i.e. network capacity) and has minimal computational overhead. In addition to using EWC to protect previously-acquired knowledge, we used the RL domain to address a broader set of requirements that are needed for successful continual learning systems: in particular, higher-level mechanisms are needed to infer which task is currently being performed, detect and incorporate novel tasks as they are encountered, and allow for rapid and ﬂexible switching between tasks [Collins and Frank, 2013]. In the primate brain, the prefrontal cortex is widely viewed as supporting these capabilities by sustaining neural representations of task context that exert top- down gating inﬂuences on sensory processing, working memory, and action selection in lower-level regions [O’Reilly and Frank, 2006, Mante et al., 2013, Miller and Cohen, 2001, Doya et al., 2002]. Inspired by this evidence, we used an agent very similar to that described in [van Hasselt et al., 2016] with few differences: (a) a network with more parameters, (b) a smaller transition table, (c) task-speciﬁc bias and gains at each layer, (d) the full action set in Atari, (e) a task-recognition model, and (e) the EWC penalty. Full details of hyper-parameters are described in Appendix app:atari. Here we brieﬂy describe the two most important modiﬁcations to the agent: the task-recognition module, and the implementation of the EWC penalty. We treat the task context as the latent variable of a Hidden Markov Model. Each task is therefore associated to an underlying generative model of the observations. The main distinguishing feature of our approach is that we allow for the addition of new generative models if they explain recent data better than the existing pool of models by using a training procedure inspired by the forget me not process[Kieran et al., 2016] (see Appendix 4.2). In order to apply EWC, we compute the Fisher information matrix at each task switch. For each task, a penalty is added with anchor point given by the current value of the parameters and with weights given by the Fisher information matrix times a scaling factor λwhich was optimized by hyperparameter search. We only added an EWC penalty to games which had experienced at least 20 million frames. We also allowed the DQN agents to maintain separate short-term memory buffers for each inferred task: these allow action values for each task to be learned off-policy using an experience replay mechanism [Mnih et al., 2015]. As such, the overall system has memory on two time-scales: over short time-scales, the experience replay mechanism allows learning in DQN to be based on the interleaved and uncorrelated experiences [Mnih et al., 2015]. At longer time scales, know-how across tasks is consolidated by using EWC. Finally, we allowed a small number of network parameters to be game-speciﬁc, rather than shared across games. In particular, we allowed each layer of the network to have biases and per element multiplicative gains that were speciﬁc to each game. We compare the performance of agents which use EWC (red) with ones that do not (blue) over sets of ten games in Figure 3. We measure the performance as the total human-normalized score across all ten games. We average across random seeds and over the choice of which ten games were played (see Appendix 4.2). We also clip the human-normalized score for each game to 1. Our measure of performance is therefore a number with a maximum of 10 (at least at human level on all games) where 0 means the agent is as good as a random agent. If we rely on plain gradient descent methods as in [Mnih et al., 2015], the agent never learns to play more than one game and the harm inﬂicted by forgetting the old games means that the total human-normalized score remains below one. By using EWC, however, the agents do indeed learn to play multiple games. As a control, we also considered the beneﬁt to the agent if we explicitly provided the agent with the true task label (Figure 3B, brown), rather than relying on the learned task recognition through the FMN algorithm (red). While augmenting the DQN agent with EWC allows it to learn many games in sequence without suffering from catastrophic forgetting, it does not reach the score that would have been obtained by training ten separate DQNs (see Figure 1 in Appendix 4.2). One possible reason for this is that we consolidated weights for each game based on a tractable approximation of parameter uncertainty, the Fisher Information. We therefore sought to test the quality of our estimates empirically. To do so, we trained an agent on a single game, and measured how perturbing the network parameters affected the agent’s score. Regardless of which game the agent was trained on, we observed the same patterns, shown in Figure 3C. First, the agent was always more robust to parameter perturbations shaped by the inverse of the diagonal of the Fisher Information (blue), as opposed to uniform perturbations (black). This validates that the diagonal of the Fisher is a good estimate of how important a certain parameter is. Within our approximation, perturbing in the nullspace should have no effect on performance at all on performance. Empirically, however, we observe that perturbing in this space (orange) has the same effect as perturbing in the inverse Fisher space. This suggests that we are over-conﬁdent about certain parameters being unimportant: it is therefore likely that the chief limitation of the current implementation is that it under-estimates parameter uncertainty. 3 Discussion We present a novel algorithm, elastic weight consolidation, that addresses the signiﬁcant problem continual learning poses for neural networks. EWC allows knowledge of previous tasks to be protected during new learning, thereby avoiding catastrophic forgetting of old abilities. It does so by selectively decreasing the plasticity of weights, and thus has parallels with neurobiological models of synaptic consolidation. We implement EWC as a soft, quadratic constraint whereby each weight is pulled back towards its old values by an amount proportional to its importance for performance on previously-learnt tasks. To the extent that tasks share structure, networks trained with EWC reuse shared components of the network. We further show that EWC can be effectively combined with deep neural networks to support continual learning in challenging reinforcement learning scenarios, such as Atari 2600 games. The EWC algorithm can be grounded in Bayesian approaches to learning. Formally, when there is a new task to be learnt, the network parameters are tempered by a prior which is the posterior distribution on the parameters given data from previous task(s). This enables fast learning rates on parameters that are poorly constrained by the previous tasks, and slow learning rates for those which are crucial. 6There has been previous work [French and Chater, 2002, Eaton and Ruvolo, 2013] using a quadratic penalty to approximate old parts of the dataset, but these applications have been limited to small models. Speciﬁcally, [French and Chater, 2002] used random inputs to compute a quadratic approxi- mation to the energy surface. Their approach is slow, as it requires re-computing the curvature at each sample. The ELLA algorithm described in [Eaton and Ruvolo, 2013] requires computing and inverting matrices with a dimensionality equal to the number of parameters being optimized, therefore it has been mainly applied to linear and logistic regressions. In contrast, EWC has a run time which is linear in both the number of parameters and the number of training examples. We could only achieve this low computational complexity by making several simpliﬁcations, most notably by approximating the posterior distribution of the parameters on a task (i.e. the weight uncertainties) by a factorized Gaussian, and by computing its variance using a point-estimate of the parameters, via the diagonal of the Fisher Information matrix. Despite its low computational cost and empirical successes—even in the setting of challenging RL domains—our use of a point estimate of the posterior’s variance (as in a Laplace approximation) does constitute a signiﬁcant weakness (see Fig 4C). Our initial explorations suggest that one might improve on this local estimate by using Bayesian neural networks [Blundell et al., 2015]. While this paper has primarily focused on building an algorithm out of neurobiological observations, it is also instructive to consider whether the algorithm’s successes can feed back into our understanding of the brain. In particular, we see considerable parallels between EWC and two computational theories of synaptic plasticity. In this respect, the perspective we offer here aligns with a recent proposal that each synapse not only stores its current weight, but also an implicit representation of its uncertainty about that weight [Aitchison and Latham, 2015]. This idea is grounded in observations that post-synaptic potentials are highly variable in amplitude (suggestive of sampling from the weight posterior during computation), and that those synapses which are more variable are more amenable to potentiation or depression (suggestive of updating the weight posterior). While we do not explore the computational beneﬁts of sampling from a posterior here, our work aligns with the notion that weight uncertainty should inform learning rates. We take this one step further, to emphasize that consolidating the high precision weights enables continual learning over long time scales. With EWC, three values have to be stored for each synapse: the weight itself, its variance and its mean. Interestingly, synapses in the brain also carry more than one piece of information. For example, the state of the short-term plasticity could carry information on the variance [Aitchison and Latham, 2015, Pﬁster et al., 2010]. The weight for the early phase of plasticity [Clopath et al., 2008] could encode the current synaptic strength, whereas the weight associated with the late-phase of plasticity or the consolidated phase could encode the mean weight. The ability to learn tasks in succession without forgetting is a core component of biological and artiﬁcial intelligence. In this work we show that an algorithm that supports continual learning—which takes inspiration from neurobiological models of synaptic consolidation—can be combined with deep neural networks to achieve successful performance in a range of challenging domains. In doing so, we demonstrate that current neurobiological theories concerning synaptic consolidation do indeed scale to large-scale learning systems. This provides prima facie evidence that these principles may be fundamental aspects of learning and memory in the brain. Acknowledgements. We would like to thank P. Dayan, D. Wierstra, S. The most signiﬁcant departure from the published models is the automatic determination of the task. We model each task by a generative model of the environment. In this work, for simplicity, we only model the current observation. The current task is modelled as a categorical contextcwhich is treated as the hidden variable in an Hidden Markov Model that explain observations. In such a model the probabilty of being in a particular context cat time tevolves according to: p(c,t + 1) = ∑ c′ p(c′,t)Γ(c,c′) Γ(c,c′) = δ(c,c′)(1 −α) + (1−δ(c,c′))α where δis the Kronecker delta function andαis the probability of switching context. The task context then conditions a generative model predicting the observation probability p(o|c,t). Given such generative models, the probability of being in a task set at time tcan be inferred by the observations seen so far as: p(c|o1...ot) ∝ ∑ c′ Γ(c,c′) p(c′,t −1)p(o|c,t) The maximal probability context is then taken to be the current task label. In our implementation, the generative models consist of factored multinomial distributions explaining the probability of the state of each pixel in the observation space. The model is a parametrized Dirichlet distribution, which summarizes the data seen so far using Bayesian updates. In order to encourage each model to specialize, we train the models as follows. We partition time into windows of a particular width W. During each window, all the Dirichlet priors are updated with the evidence seen so far. At the end of the window, the model best corresponding to the current task set is selected. Since this model was the most useful to explain the current data, it keeps its prior, while all other priors are reverted to their state at the beginning of the time window. We ensure that one hold-out uniform (i.e. uninitialized) Dirichlet-multinomial is always available. Whenever the hold-out model is selected a new generative model is created and a new task context is therefore created. This model is Bayesian, in the sense that data is used to maintain beliefs over priors on the generative models, and is non-parametric, in the sense that the model can grow in function of the observed data. It can be seen as an implementation of the ﬂat forget me not algorithm described in [Kieran et al., 2016]. The parameter αis not learnt. Instead we use the result from [Veness et al., 2012] where it is shown that a time decaying switch rate α= 1/tguarantees good worst case asymptotic perfmance provided the number of tasks grows as o ( n log n ) . new_method.method:
Open Problems: Current continual-learning (CL) systems—even those that use replay, parameter-isolation, or mode-connectivity—assume the task order is immutable.  Yet on every public benchmark large swings in forgetting are caused by unlucky task permutations.  For 1–3 B parameter backbones the cost of a bad order is huge (days of GPU time) and replay buffers large enough to mask this effect are prohibitive.  No existing work delivers an on-the-fly curriculum that (1) is model-agnostic, (2) scales to billion-scale transformers, and (3) uses both data-set similarity and gradient interference to decide which task to train next.  Solving “online task-ordering” would directly reduce catastrophic forgetting without extra memory and would make continual pre-training of foundation models far more practical.
Methods: We propose Dynamic Curriculum Ordering with Dual Signals (DyCLOS).
1. Lightweight task fingerprinting: When a new task Ti arrives we form a 512-sample probe set.  Two signals are computed:
   a) Data similarity Sdata(Ti,Tj) to all previous tasks with the Gaussian OTDD distance in a shared frozen embedding space (we reuse the backbone’s tokenizer + first transformer block to avoid extra encoders).
   b) Gradient interference Sint(Ti,Tj) = E[ cos(gTi , gTj) ] where g are per-sample gradients on the probe; computed with efficient back-prop accumulation and grad-sketching.
2. Curriculum graph construction: Each task becomes a node; edge weight w(Ti,Tj)=α·Sdata+β·max(0,−Sint) (α,β learned by Bayesian optimisation on a held-out stream).  We maintain an incremental minimum-cost Hamiltonian path prefix; when a new task arrives we insert it at the position that minimises cumulative expected forgetting ∑w along the path.
3. Windowed re-ordering: Because future tasks are unknown, DyCLOS keeps a sliding window of size k (e.g., 4) of untrained tasks and solves the path locally with a fast beam search; already-trained tasks are fixed, guaranteeing bounded compute.
4. Parameter-efficient adaptation: Training follows Additive Parameter Decomposition + LoRA (APD-LoRA).  Only rank-32 adapters in attention/MLP and sparse task-adaptive vectors are updated (≈0.8 % of parameters).  This keeps gradient evaluation cheap so probe computation is negligible (<3 % extra FLOPs).
5. Stability-aware inner loop: We adopt the continual-evaluation mask of Kühn et al. to detect stability gaps; if a >5 % temporary drop is seen we lower the inner-loop learning rate for that task slice.
6. Reproducibility toolkit: Code is built on PyTorch + DeepSpeed-ZeRO-3, logs hash of data splits, records FLOPs & wall-time, and publishes full hyper-parameter sweeps via JSON-Schema.
Experimental Setup: Backbones: LLaMA-1 1.3 B and ViT-g/14 (1.8 B CLIP) to show modality-agnosticism.
Benchmarks:
• CTrL vision streams (Sin,Sout,S+,S− ,Slong)
• FoMo-in-Flux multimodal 20-step stream
• Split-Reddit-QA (new 50-task NLP stream, released by us)
Baselines: Finetune, ER-Reservoir, APD, MC-SGD, LoRA-replay, Model-Merge, and a fixed heuristic ordering (chronological).
Metrics:
• Ωacc (average accuracy after last task)
• Ωforg (average forgetting)
• Transfer-Gain (as in MNTDP)
• Compute-overhead (% extra GPU hours vs. fixed order)
Ablations:
(i) similarity only, (ii) interference only, (iii) no re-ordering (random), (iv) window size, (v) adapter vs. full fine-tune.
Robustness: repeat each stream with 5 random seeds; add synthetic noisy task to test mis-classification of similarity.
Result: We expect DyCLOS to:
• Improve Ωacc by 3-5 pp and reduce Ωforg by 40-60 % relative to the best fixed-order baseline on all three backbones.
• Show positive Transfer-Gain (>0) on Sin and S+ streams where fixed baselines yield negative transfer.
• Add ≤5 % extra GPU compute over the whole stream (probe + beam search).
• Ablations reveal that combining both signals is critical (single-signal variants recover only ~50 % of the gain).
Conclusion: DyCLOS turns task-ordering—from a nuisance hyper-parameter into a controllable lever—yielding sizeable forgetting reductions at almost no memory cost and without replay scaling.  The method is generic (works for language and vision), compatible with any parameter-efficient learner, and, because it relies only on small probes, adds trivial overhead even for 3 B-scale models.  Beyond academic impact (first practical solution to online task scheduling) it offers practitioners a plug-and-play curriculum layer for continual pre-training pipelines.  Future work can extend the graph criterion with privacy or fairness terms and explore joint optimisation of ordering and adapter capacity, opening a path to fully autonomous lifelong foundation models.

experimental_design.experiment_strategy:
Below are three complementary, feasible experiments to validate DyCLOS. Each includes: datasets and task streams, models and training setup (with APD-LoRA-style parameter-efficient adaptation), how to compute DyCLOS signals and ordering, baselines, metrics, ablations, and minimal Python scaffolding for core components (signals, scheduler, and training loop) you can drop into a PyTorch project.

---
Experiment 1: Controlled sanity-check with synthetic interference (vision)
Goal: Show DyCLOS actually learns to prefer orders that avoid negative transfer, and that both data-similarity and gradient-interference signals matter. Use a small, fast setup where the ground-truth interference structure is known.

Setup
- Data/Tasks (10 tasks, 512-probe each):
  1–4: Rotated-MNIST 10-way classification at 0°, 15°, 30°, 45° (high similarity, low interference)
  5–7: Rotated-MNIST at 75°, 90°, 105° (moderate similarity, higher interference vs 1–4)
  8: Permuted-MNIST (low similarity, high interference)
  9: Same images as task 2 (15°) with random labels (synthetic noisy task) to test DyCLOS’ robustness
  10: Fashion-MNIST 10-way (low similarity, moderate interference)
- Model: ViT-Tiny or ViT-S/16 (timm), pre-trained on ImageNet-1k.
- Adaptation: LoRA r=16 on attention and MLP projections; optional additive task vector (APD) with 0.1 sparsity on FFN biases.
- Optimizer: AdamW, base LR 1e-4, wd 0.01; batch 128; 3 epochs per task.
- DyCLOS specifics: window k=4, beam size b=6, α=β=1 (or small 2×2 grid search on a held-out mini-stream). Probe = 512 examples per task.

Baselines
- Finetune (fixed order = chronological or random permutation) 
- ER-Reservoir (buffer 512) + LoRA
- APD (without ordering)
- LoRA-replay (buffer 512)
- Random ordering (no signals) and similarity-only, interference-only ablations

Metrics
- Ωacc: average accuracy across tasks after last task
- Ωforg: average forgetting
- Transfer-Gain (MNTDP-style: improvement over training each task in isolation)
- Compute-overhead: (probe+ordering time)/total training time

Why this validates
- The designed stream contains known high-similarity blocks and explicit interference (permute/noise). DyCLOS should schedule 1–4 early, postpone 8–9, and minimize transitions that incur high cost, reducing Ωforg with minimal overhead.

Expected outcome
- +3–5 pp Ωacc vs best fixed order; 40–60% Ωforg reduction
- ≤5% compute overhead; ablations recover ~50% of full gain

---
Experiment 2: Scaled vision continual-learning benchmark (CIFAR-100 CIL)
Goal: Demonstrate DyCLOS’ practical benefit on a standard CL setting and show compute-overhead remains small.

Setup
- Data/Tasks: CIFAR-100 split into 10 tasks × 10 classes each (class-incremental). Create 5 independent random task permutations. 512-probe per task.
- Model: ViT-B/16 (timm) pretrained on ImageNet-21k; train linear head + LoRA (r=16) in attention/MLP; optionally APD sparse task vector on selected FFN layers.
- DyCLOS: window k=4, beam b=8, α,β tuned on 1 held-out seed by BO (e.g., skopt) for ≤20 trials using a 3-task toy stream to bound compute. Use Gaussian OTDD in ViT’s frozen token-embed + first encoder block; Sint via grad-cosine on LoRA params.
- Training: 5 epochs per task, batch 256, 224×224 resize, RandAugment, AdamW (1e-4).

Baselines
- Finetune, ER-Reservoir (buffer 2k), APD, MC-SGD (mode connectivity SGD), LoRA-replay, Model-Merge, and chronological ordering heuristic.

Metrics and protocol
- Report Ωacc, Ωforg, Transfer-Gain, overhead per seed; average over 5 seeds. Validate on full test sets per task after each task.
- Robustness: include one noisy duplicate task (random labels) inserted at position 5 across seeds to test misclassification handling.

Why this validates
- Standard CIL emphasizes forgetting without huge memory. DyCLOS should prefer local orders within the window that minimize transitions with high w(Ti,Tj), improving final average accuracy while keeping overhead low.

Expected outcome
- DyCLOS outperforms best fixed ordering by 3–5 pp on Ωacc and halves Ωforg, with ≤5% overhead.

---
Experiment 3: Multi-dataset NLP stream (text classification)
Goal: Show modality-agnosticism and that DyCLOS’ signals remain informative when using a language backbone.

Setup
- Data/Tasks (12 tasks): SST-2, IMDB, Yelp Polarity, Amazon Polarity, AG News, DBPedia, TREC-6, Emotion, Banking77, HateXplain (binary), TweetEval-Sentiment, Yahoo Answers (subset). Reserve 512-sample probe per task.
- Model: RoBERTa-base (or DeBERTa-v3-base) with LoRA r=16 on attention + FFN; task-specific classification head per task.
- DyCLOS: window k=4, beam b=6, α,β tuned on a small 4-task held-out stream (≤15 trials). Embeddings from tokenizer + first transformer block (frozen). Sint via grad-cosine on LoRA parameters with grad-sketch to 1024 dims.
- Training: AdamW 2e-5, batch 64, 3 epochs per task; stability-aware inner loop: if running mean validation over seen tasks drops >5% for this task, reduce LR by 0.5 for remaining steps.

Baselines
- Finetune, ER-Reservoir (buffer 2k), APD, LoRA-replay, Model-Merge, chronological order.

Metrics
- Ωacc, Ωforg, Transfer-Gain, overhead; 5 seeds with random task permutations.

Why this validates
- Highlights cross-task similarity/interference in language domain and shows DyCLOS’ genericity. Probes are inexpensive vs training; ordering should reduce forgetting without replay scaling.

Expected outcome
- Similar gains as vision; ablations show combining Sdata and Sint is necessary to recover full gains.

---
Core implementation snippets (drop-in-ready)
Note: These are minimal and work with any torch model; adapt the model hooks to your LoRA/APD implementation. For clarity we use average-grad approximation plus optional grad-sketch; the Gaussian OTDD follows the closed-form 2-Wasserstein distance between Gaussians.

1) Gaussian OTDD (frozen first block embeddings)

import torch, math

def gaussian_w2(emb1, emb2, eps=1e-5):
    # emb: [N,d] float32
    m1, m2 = emb1.mean(0), emb2.mean(0)
    X1 = emb1 - m1
    X2 = emb2 - m2
    # covariances with small ridge for stability
    C1 = (X1.t() @ X1) / max(1, emb1.shape[0]-1) + eps * torch.eye(emb1.shape[1], device=emb1.device)
    C2 = (X2.t() @ X2) / max(1, emb2.shape[0]-1) + eps * torch.eye(emb2.shape[1], device=emb2.device)
    # sqrt(C1)
    U, S, Vh = torch.linalg.svd(C1)
    C1_sqrt = (U * S.clamp_min(0).sqrt()) @ U.t()
    middle = C1_sqrt @ C2 @ C1_sqrt
    U2, S2, _ = torch.linalg.svd(middle)
    tr_term = torch.trace(C1 + C2 - 2 * (U2 * S2.clamp_min(0).sqrt()) @ U2.t())
    mean_term = torch.sum((m1 - m2) ** 2)
    return (mean_term + tr_term).clamp_min(0).sqrt()  # W2

@torch.no_grad()
def task_fingerprint_embeddings(model, first_block, dataloader, max_samples=512):
    # first_block: module that maps tokens/images to first hidden block output
    embs = []
    n = 0
    for x, y in dataloader:
        x = x.to(next(model.parameters()).device)
        h = first_block(x)
        # pool: mean over sequence/patch dimension if needed
        if h.dim() == 3:  # [B, T, d]
            h = h.mean(1)
        embs.append(h.detach())
        n += h.size(0)
        if n >= max_samples:
            break
    return torch.cat(embs, dim=0)[:max_samples]

2) Gradient interference via cosine similarity with grad-sketch

import torch

def flatten_grads(params):
    return torch.cat([p.grad.detach().reshape(-1) for p in params if p.grad is not None])

@torch.no_grad()
def random_projection_matrix(D, d_proj=1024, device="cpu"):
    R = torch.randn(D, d_proj, device=device)
    R /= math.sqrt(D)
    return R

def average_grad_vector(model, params, dataloader, loss_fn, max_batches=8):
    device = next(model.parameters()).device
    for p in model.parameters():
        if p.grad is not None:
            p.grad = None
    n = 0
    g_sum = None
    for i, (x, y) in enumerate(dataloader):
        if i >= max_batches: break
        x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
        out = model(x)
        loss = loss_fn(out, y) / (max_batches)
        loss.backward()
        n += 1
    g = flatten_grads(params)
    return g  # gradient of accumulated micro-batches

def cosine_interference(model, params, dl_i, dl_j, loss_fn, proj_dim=1024, max_batches=8):
    gi = average_grad_vector(model, params, dl_i, loss_fn, max_batches)
    gj = average_grad_vector(model, params, dl_j, loss_fn, max_batches)
    D = gi.numel()
    device = gi.device
    if proj_dim > 0 and D > proj_dim:
        R = random_projection_matrix(D, proj_dim, device=device)
        gi = gi @ R
        gj = gj @ R
    cos = torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity(gi, gj, dim=0).item()
    return cos  # Sint ≈ E[cos]

3) Curriculum graph and windowed beam-search insertion

from itertools import permutations

class DyCLOSScheduler:
    def __init__(self, alpha=1.0, beta=1.0, window_k=4, beam_size=6):
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.beta = beta
        self.window_k = window_k
        self.beam = beam_size
        self.trained_prefix = []     # fixed order already trained
        self.untrained_queue = []    # incoming tasks waiting
        self.cost_cache = {}         # (i,j) -> cost

    def edge_cost(self, i, j):
        # i, j are task ids; relies on precomputed Sdata[i][j], Sint[i][j]
        key = (i,j)
        if key in self.cost_cache:
            return self.cost_cache[key]
        sdata = self.Sdata[i][j]
        sint = self.Sint[i][j]
        w = self.alpha * sdata + self.beta * max(0.0, -sint)
        self.cost_cache[key] = w
        return w

    def path_cost(self, path):
        return sum(self.edge_cost(path[t], path[t+1]) for t in range(len(path)-1))

    def update_signals(self, Sdata, Sint):
        self.Sdata = Sdata
        self.Sint = Sint

    def insert_task(self, task_id):
        self.untrained_queue.append(task_id)
        # if we have >= k tasks queued, solve local window
        while len(self.untrained_queue) >= self.window_k:
            window = self.untrained_queue[:self.window_k]
            best_seq = None
            best_cost = float('inf')
            # beam-search over local permutations
            cand_paths = [[t] for t in window]
            for _ in range(1, len(window)):
                new_cands = []
                for path in cand_paths:
                    rem = [t for t in window if t not in path]
                    for t in rem:
                        new_cands.append(path + [t])
                # prune by beam using local path cost + link to prefix end if any
                def full_cost(p):
                    cost = 0.0
                    if self.trained_prefix:
                        cost += self.edge_cost(self.trained_prefix[-1], p[0])
                    cost += self.path_cost(p)
                    return cost
                cand_paths = sorted(new_cands, key=full_cost)[:self.beam]
            # choose best candidate
            def full_cost_final(p):
                cost = 0.0
                if self.trained_prefix:
                    cost += self.edge_cost(self.trained_prefix[-1], p[0])
                cost += self.path_cost(p)
                return cost
            best_seq = min(cand_paths, key=full_cost_final)
            # commit first in window, keep rest queued
            chosen = best_seq[0]
            self.trained_prefix.append(chosen)
            self.untrained_queue.remove(chosen)
        return list(self.trained_prefix) + list(self.untrained_queue)

4) Training loop skeleton with stability-aware inner loop and Ω metrics

import time
from collections import defaultdict

class ContinualTrainer:
    def __init__(self, model, lora_params, optimizer, loss_fn, eval_fn, scheduler, task_dataloaders):
        self.model = model
        self.lora_params = lora_params
        self.opt = optimizer
        self.loss_fn = loss_fn
        self.eval_fn = eval_fn
        self.sched = scheduler
        self.task_dls = task_dataloaders  # dict task_id -> (train_dl, probe_dl, val_dl, test_dl)
        self.test_acc_hist = defaultdict(list)  # task_id -> list over time
        self.best_seen = defaultdict(lambda: 0.0)

    def compute_signals_for_new_task(self, new_task_id, task_ids):
        # Build Sdata and Sint entries involving new_task_id only
        device = next(self.model.parameters()).device
        # embeddings
        emb_new = task_fingerprint_embeddings(self.model, self.first_block, self.task_dls[new_task_id][1])
        for t in task_ids:
            emb_t = task_fingerprint_embeddings(self.model, self.first_block, self.task_dls[t][1])
            sdata = gaussian_w2(emb_new, emb_t).item()
            self.sched.Sdata[new_task_id][t] = sdata
            self.sched.Sdata[t][new_task_id] = sdata
        # gradient interference (symmetrize by mean of pairwise cos)
        for t in task_ids:
            cos = cosine_interference(self.model, self.lora_params, self.task_dls[new_task_id][1], self.task_dls[t][1], self.loss_fn)
            self.sched.Sint[new_task_id][t] = cos
            self.sched.Sint[t][new_task_id] = cos

    def train_task(self, task_id, epochs=3, lr=1e-4):
        train_dl, _, val_dl, _ = self.task_dls[task_id]
        device = next(self.model.parameters()).device
        # set LR for this task
        for g in self.opt.param_groups:
            g['lr'] = lr
        running_drop_triggered = False
        base_mean = self.mean_val_acc_over_seen()
        for ep in range(epochs):
            self.model.train()
            for x, y in train_dl:
                x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
                self.opt.zero_grad()
                out = self.model(x)
                loss = self.loss_fn(out, y)
                loss.backward()
                self.opt.step()
            # stability-aware check
            mean_after = self.mean_val_acc_over_seen(extra_task=task_id)
            if not running_drop_triggered and base_mean - mean_after > 0.05 * max(base_mean, 1e-6):
                # reduce LR for remaining epochs
                for g in self.opt.param_groups:
                    g['lr'] *= 0.5
                running_drop_triggered = True
        # evaluate after training this task
        self.evaluate_all_seen()

    def evaluate_all_seen(self):
        self.model.eval()
        for t, (_, _, _, test_dl) in self.task_dls.items():
            if t not in self.seen_tasks: continue
            acc = self.eval_fn(self.model, test_dl)
            self.test_acc_hist[t].append(acc)
            self.best_seen[t] = max(self.best_seen[t], acc)

    @property
    def seen_tasks(self):
        return set(self.sched.trained_prefix)

    def mean_val_acc_over_seen(self, extra_task=None):
        # naive: reuse test as proxy; replace with proper val
        if extra_task is not None:
            tasks = list(self.seen_tasks | {extra_task})
        else:
            tasks = list(self.seen_tasks)
        if not tasks: return 0.0
        accs = []
        self.model.eval()
        for t in tasks:
            accs.append(self.eval_fn(self.model, self.task_dls[t][2]))
        return sum(accs) / len(accs)

    def compute_metrics(self):
        # Ωacc: average last accuracy across tasks
        last_accs = [self.test_acc_hist[t][-1] for t in self.seen_tasks]
        omega_acc = sum(last_accs) / max(1, len(last_accs))
        # Ωforg: average forgetting = best_past - last
        forg = []
        for t in self.seen_tasks:
            last = self.test_acc_hist[t][-1]
            best = max(self.test_acc_hist[t])
            forg.append(max(0.0, best - last))
        omega_forg = sum(forg) / max(1, len(forg))
        return omega_acc, omega_forg

5) Putting it together for one stream (pseudo-pipeline)

# Assume: model, first_block, lora_params, optimizer, loss_fn, eval_fn prepared
# task_dls: dict task_id -> (train_dl, probe_dl, val_dl, test_dl)

from collections import defaultdict

Sdata = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(float))
Sint  = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(float))
scheduler = DyCLOSScheduler(alpha=1.0, beta=1.0, window_k=4, beam_size=6)
scheduler.update_signals(Sdata, Sint)
trainer = ContinualTrainer(model, lora_params, optimizer, loss_fn, eval_fn, scheduler, task_dls)
trainer.first_block = first_block

start = time.perf_counter()
for new_task in incoming_task_stream:  # e.g., shuffled list of task_ids
    trainer.compute_signals_for_new_task(new_task, task_ids=list(scheduler.trained_prefix + scheduler.untrained_queue))
    order_now = scheduler.insert_task(new_task)
    # if a new task has been fixed to prefix (committed), train it
    # In this simple loop, we train immediately after insertion when it gets committed
    while len(scheduler.trained_prefix) > len(trainer.seen_tasks):
        t_to_train = scheduler.trained_prefix[-1]
        trainer.train_task(t_to_train, epochs=3, lr=1e-4)
end = time.perf_counter()
probe_and_order_overhead = end - start  # compare to pure training time baseline
omega_acc, omega_forg = trainer.compute_metrics()

---
Ablation toggles to include in all experiments
- similarity only: set beta=0
- interference only: set alpha=0
- random: bypass scheduler and use arriving order or shuffle
- window size: set window_k ∈ {2, 3, 4, 6}
- adapter vs full FT: swap LoRA params with all params (note the compute baseline)

Compute tips for feasibility
- Use mixed precision (torch.cuda.amp) and gradient accumulation to fit larger batch sizes.
- For language, quantize base weights with bitsandbytes 8-bit while keeping LoRA in 16-bit.
- Keep probe dataloaders small, max 512 samples; set max_batches=8 for gradient interference.

What to report
- For each experiment, a table of Ωacc, Ωforg, Transfer-Gain, overhead with 95% CIs over 5 seeds.
- Schedule visualizations: task order chosen by DyCLOS vs random, with edge costs per transition.
- Time breakdown: percent of total time spent in probes + scheduling.

These three experiments jointly validate DyCLOS’ effectiveness: controlled synthetic interference (E1), practical vision CIL (E2), and language modality (E3). They emphasize reduced forgetting and improved final accuracy with negligible overhead, and ablations confirm the necessity of both signals and local reordering.
experimental_design.experiment_details:
Below is a complete, implementation-ready plan aligned to the Experiment Strategy, with thorough details for each experiment, cross-experiment integration, reliability measures, and PyTorch-first code scaffolding that reuses established libraries (timm, transformers, peft, POT, optuna/skopt, avalanche, torchmetrics, deepspeed). The design minimizes redundant experiments while ensuring comprehensive validation of DyCLOS.

Shared implementation notes (applies to all experiments)
- Core libraries
  - PyTorch ≥ 2.1, torchvision, timm (vision backbones), transformers + peft (NLP + LoRA/IA3), avalanche-lib (baselines like ER, strategies, and benchmark creation for CIL), POT (Python Optimal Transport) for Sinkhorn distances, optuna (Bayesian optimization), torchmetrics (metrics), wandb or MLflow (logging), deepspeed (optional), bitsandbytes (optional 8-bit for language), numpy, scipy.
- Reproducibility toolkit
  - Seed everything: torch.manual_seed, numpy.random.seed, random.seed; set torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic=True, benchmark=False.
  - Log: config JSON (hyperparameters, seeds, task permutations), code commit hash, dataset version/hash, FLOPs/step (optional: deepspeed flops estimator or torch.profiler), wall-time, GPU type.
  - Report 95% CIs over 5 seeds; use paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for DyCLOS vs best fixed-order baseline and compute Cliff’s delta effect sizes.
- Parameter-efficient adaptation (APD-LoRA operationalization)
  - LoRA: peft LoraConfig(r=16–32, alpha=32–64, dropout=0.05). Target attention and MLP Linear layers (vision) or attention/FFN (NLP). Only LoRA params and task heads trainable.
  - Task-adaptive vectors: PEFT IA3 (multiplicative adapter) as a sparse capacity adjunct to LoRA; this matches the spirit of APD (low-overhead task-specific vectors) without reimplementing APD from scratch. Keep total trainable params ≈ 0.6–0.9%.
  - Optionally enable gradient checkpointing to keep probe cost low; ensure LoRA parameter gradients are always enabled.
- DyCLOS signals and scheduling
  - Data-similarity Sdata: compute in a frozen shared embedding space built from the tokenizer + first transformer block (NLP) or patch-embed + first encoder block (ViT). Compute either:
    - Fast Gaussian W2 approximation (closed-form 2-Wasserstein between Gaussian-fitted embeddings), or
    - Sinkhorn OT distance between empirical embeddings with POT for higher fidelity (recommended for E2/E3; cap samples at 512 for probes).
  - Gradient interference Sint: cosine similarity of average gradient vectors on LoRA/IA3 params using a small number of micro-batches (e.g., 8). For stability and speed, project to 1024 dims via a fixed random Gaussian sketch (Johnson–Lindenstrauss) before cosine.
  - Edge weight: w(Ti,Tj) = α·Sdata + β·max(0, −Sint). α,β tuned via Bayesian optimization on a small held-out stream (≤20 trials) to bound compute.
  - Scheduler: sliding window of size k (e.g., 4), beam search size b (6–8), commit the first task in local min-cost path; already-trained prefix is fixed.
- Stability-aware inner loop
  - Maintain running mean validation across seen tasks. If new-task training drops the mean >5% relative to preceding snapshot, reduce LR by 0.5 for the remainder of the task training. This is cheap and increases stability.
- Metrics
  - Ωacc: mean of the final accuracy across all tasks after the last task.
  - Ωforg: average forgetting = mean over tasks of (max historical accuracy on that task − final accuracy, clipped at 0).
  - Transfer-Gain (MNTDP-like): average improvement per task relative to training the task in isolation with the same adapter setup and compute.
  - Compute-overhead: extra GPU hours (probe + scheduling + BO tuning for α,β amortized) vs. fixed-order baseline.


Experiment 1: Controlled sanity-check with synthetic interference (vision)
Goal
- Validate that DyCLOS learns an order that avoids negative transfer. Show both Sdata and Sint matter via ablations. Use a small, fast setup with known interference structure.

Data/Tasks
- 10 tasks, each with 512-sample probe:
  1–4: Rotated-MNIST 0°, 15°, 30°, 45° (high similarity, low interference among themselves)
  5–7: Rotated-MNIST 75°, 90°, 105° (moderate similarity, higher interference vs 1–4)
  8: Permuted-MNIST (low similarity, high interference to earlier tasks)
  9: Noisy task: same images as task 2 (15°) with random labels (tests robustness to misleading similarity)
  10: Fashion-MNIST (low similarity, moderate interference)
- Splits: 45k/5k train/val, 10k test per task where applicable; for permuted/noisy, maintain equal sizes.

Model and Training
- Model: ViT-S/16 or ViT-Tiny from timm pretrained on ImageNet-1k.
- Adaptation: LoRA r=16 on attention qkv and proj, and MLP fc1/fc2; add IA3 for MLP layers (PEFT). Task-specific linear classification head per task.
- Hyperparameters: AdamW lr=1e-4, wd=0.01, batch=128, 3 epochs per task, input size 224×224 (bilinear upsample), RandAugment(n=1, m=7) minimal.
- Mixed precision with torch.cuda.amp.autocast; gradient accumulation if needed.

DyCLOS specifics
- Window k=4, beam b=6. α=β=1 by default. Optional tiny grid search α,β ∈ {0.5, 1.0, 2.0} on a held-out 3-task micro-stream.
- Probes: 512 examples per task; max 8 micro-batches for Sint.
- Sdata: Gaussian W2 for speed; verify with Sinkhorn on 25% of pairs for a sanity check.

Baselines
- Finetune (fixed arrival order; also evaluate 3 random permutations).
- ER-Reservoir (buffer=512) with LoRA; avalanche ExperienceReplay.
- APD/IA3-only (no ordering) using PEFT.
- LoRA-replay (buffer=512).
- Random ordering (no signals); similarity-only (β=0); interference-only (α=0).

Metrics
- Ωacc, Ωforg, Transfer-Gain, Compute-overhead.
- Report 5 seeds with distinct task permutations; confidence intervals; significance tests.

Why this validates
- The stream encodes known structure (1–4 similar, 8 and 9 harmful). DyCLOS should schedule 1–4 early, postpone 8–9, and reduce forgetting with minimal overhead. Noisy task 9 checks robustness.

Expected outcome
- +3–5 pp Ωacc vs. best fixed-order; 40–60% Ωforg reduction; ≤5% overhead. Ablations recover ~50% of the gain.

Key implementation details (E1)
- Data pipelines: torchvision.datasets.MNIST and FashionMNIST; create rotation transforms per task; permuted MNIST by a fixed pixel permutation; noisy labels for task 9.
- Embeddings: timm ViT forward hook to extract outputs from the first encoder block; mean-pool over patches.

Example code snippets (E1)

1) Data creation for rotated/permuted/noisy MNIST

```python
import torch, torchvision as tv
from torchvision import transforms as T
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader
import numpy as np

class RandomLabelDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, base_ds, num_classes=10, seed=0):
        self.base = base_ds
        rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
        self.labels = rng.randint(0, num_classes, size=len(base_ds))
    def __len__(self): return len(self.base)
    def __getitem__(self, i):
        x, _ = self.base[i]
        return x, int(self.labels[i])

def make_rotated_mnist(angle, train=True):
    tfm = T.Compose([
        T.Resize(224),
        T.RandomApply([T.RandomRotation((angle, angle))], p=1.0),
        T.ToTensor(),
        T.Normalize((0.1307,), (0.3081,)),
        T.Lambda(lambda z: z.repeat(3,1,1))
    ])
    return tv.datasets.MNIST(root='data', train=train, download=True, transform=tfm)

def make_permuted_mnist(train=True, seed=0):
    base = tv.datasets.MNIST(root='data', train=train, download=True, transform=T.ToTensor())
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    perm = rng.permutation(28*28)
    def permute(img):
        x = img.view(-1)[perm].view(28,28).unsqueeze(0)
        return T.functional.resize(x, [224,224]).repeat(3,1,1)
    class PermDS(Dataset):
        def __init__(self, base): self.base=base
        def __len__(self): return len(self.base)
        def __getitem__(self, i):
            img, y = self.base[i]
            return permute(img), y
    return PermDS(base)

# Build tasks dict: id -> {train,val,test,probe}
```

import timm, torch
from peft import LoraConfig, IA3Config, get_peft_model, TaskType

vit = timm.create_model('vit_small_patch16_224', pretrained=True)

# First block embedding extractor

def embed_first_block(x):
    # x: [B,3,224,224]
    h = first_block(x)               # [B, num_patches+1, d] depending on class token

3) Sdata via Gaussian W2 (fast) or POT Sinkhorn (higher fidelity)

```python
import torch
from ot import sinkhorn2

def gaussian_w2(emb1, emb2, eps=1e-5):
    m1, m2 = emb1.mean(0), emb2.mean(0)
    X1, X2 = emb1 - m1, emb2 - m2
    C1 = (X1.t() @ X1) / max(1, emb1.shape[0]-1) + eps * torch.eye(emb1.shape[1], device=emb1.device)
    C2 = (X2.t() @ X2) / max(1, emb2.shape[0]-1) + eps * torch.eye(emb2.shape[1], device=emb2.device)
    U, S, _ = torch.linalg.svd(C1)
    C1s = (U * S.clamp_min(0).sqrt()) @ U.t()
    M = C1s @ C2 @ C1s
    U2, S2, _ = torch.linalg.svd(M)
    tr_term = torch.trace(C1 + C2 - 2 * (U2 * S2.clamp_min(0).sqrt()) @ U2.t())
    mean_term = torch.sum((m1 - m2) ** 2)
    return (mean_term + tr_term).clamp_min(0).sqrt()

@torch.no_grad()
def sinkhorn_ot(emb1, emb2, reg=0.1):
    # emb: [N,d] on CPU for POT; move small slices if needed
    x1, x2 = emb1.detach().cpu().numpy(), emb2.detach().cpu().numpy()
    n, m = x1.shape[0], x2.shape[0]
    C = ((x1[:,None,:]-x2[None,:,:])**2).sum(-1)  # squared Euclidean
    a = np.ones(n) / n; b = np.ones(m) / m
    val = sinkhorn2(a, b, C, reg)[0]  # transport cost
    return float(np.sqrt(val))
```

4) Gradient interference cosine with sketching

```python
import math, torch

def flatten_grads(params):
    return torch.cat([p.grad.detach().reshape(-1) for p in params if p.grad is not None])

@torch.no_grad()
def rand_proj(D, d_proj=1024, device='cuda'):
    R = torch.randn(D, d_proj, device=device)
    R /= math.sqrt(D)
    return R

@torch.no_grad()
def get_trainable_params(model):
    return [p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad]

def avg_grad_vec(model, params, dl, loss_fn, max_batches=8):
    device = next(model.parameters()).device
    for p in params:
        if p.grad is not None:
            p.grad.zero_()
    model.train()
    n = 0
    for i, (x,y) in enumerate(dl):
        if i >= max_batches: break
        x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
        model.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        with torch.cuda.amp.autocast():
            logits = model(x)
            loss = loss_fn(logits, y) / max_batches
        loss.backward()
        n += 1
    g = flatten_grads(params)
    return g

def cosine_interference(model, dl_i, dl_j, loss_fn, proj_dim=1024, max_batches=8):
    params = get_trainable_params(model)
    gi = avg_grad_vec(model, params, dl_i, loss_fn, max_batches)
    gj = avg_grad_vec(model, params, dl_j, loss_fn, max_batches)
    D = gi.numel(); device = gi.device
    if proj_dim > 0 and D > proj_dim:
        R = rand_proj(D, proj_dim, device)
        gi = gi @ R; gj = gj @ R
    return torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity(gi, gj, dim=0).item()
```

5) Scheduler (windowed beam search)

```python
from collections import defaultdict

class DyCLOSScheduler:
    def __init__(self, alpha=1.0, beta=1.0, window_k=4, beam_size=6):
        self.alpha, self.beta = alpha, beta
        self.window_k, self.beam = window_k, beam_size
        self.Sdata = defaultdict(dict); self.Sint = defaultdict(dict)
        self.trained_prefix = []; self.untrained_queue = []
    def edge_cost(self, i, j):
        sdata = self.Sdata[i][j]
        sint = self.Sint[i][j]
        return self.alpha * sdata + self.beta * max(0.0, -sint)
    def path_cost(self, path):
        return sum(self.edge_cost(path[t], path[t+1]) for t in range(len(path)-1))
    def insert_task(self, task_id):
        self.untrained_queue.append(task_id)
        while len(self.untrained_queue) >= self.window_k:
            window = self.untrained_queue[:self.window_k]
            cands = [[t] for t in window]
            for _ in range(1, len(window)):
                new_cands = []
                for p in cands:
                    rem = [t for t in window if t not in p]
                    for t in rem: new_cands.append(p+[t])
                def score(p):
                    cost = 0.0
                    if self.trained_prefix:
                        cost += self.edge_cost(self.trained_prefix[-1], p[0])
                    cost += self.path_cost(p)
                    return cost
                cands = sorted(new_cands, key=score)[:self.beam]
            best = min(cands, key=lambda p: (self.edge_cost(self.trained_prefix[-1], p[0]) if self.trained_prefix else 0.0)+self.path_cost(p))
            chosen = best[0]
            self.trained_prefix.append(chosen)
            self.untrained_queue.remove(chosen)
        return list(self.trained_prefix) + list(self.untrained_queue)
```

6) Training skeleton and metrics

```python
from torchmetrics.classification import MulticlassAccuracy

class ContinualTrainer:
    def __init__(self, model, optimizer, loss_fn, eval_fn, scheduler, task_dls):
        self.model, self.opt, self.loss_fn = model, optimizer, loss_fn
        self.eval_fn, self.sched, self.task_dls = eval_fn, scheduler, task_dls
        self.hist = { }  # task_id -> list of accuracies over time
        self.best_seen = {}
        self.seen = []
    def eval_task(self, task_id, split='val'):
        self.model.eval(); correct=0; total=0
        dl = self.task_dls[task_id][split]
        acc = MulticlassAccuracy(num_classes=self.task_dls[task_id]['n_classes']).to(next(self.model.parameters()).device)
        with torch.no_grad():
            for x,y in dl:
                x,y=x.to(acc.device),y.to(acc.device)
                logits=self.model(x)
                acc.update(logits, y)
        return acc.compute().item()
    def mean_val_seen(self, extra=None):
        tasks = set(self.seen)
        if extra is not None: tasks.add(extra)
        if not tasks: return 0.0
        return sum(self.eval_task(t, 'val') for t in tasks)/len(tasks)
    def train_one_task(self, task_id, epochs=3, base_lr=1e-4):
        self.seen.append(task_id)
        for g in self.opt.param_groups: g['lr']=base_lr
        dl = self.task_dls[task_id]['train']
        base_mean = self.mean_val_seen()
        lowered=False
        device = next(self.model.parameters()).device
        for ep in range(epochs):
            self.model.train()
            for x,y in dl:
                x,y=x.to(device),y.to(device)
                self.opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
                with torch.cuda.amp.autocast():
                    logits=self.model(x); loss=self.loss_fn(logits,y)
                loss.backward(); self.opt.step()
            cur = self.mean_val_seen(extra=task_id)
            if not lowered and base_mean - cur > 0.05*max(base_mean,1e-6):
                for g in self.opt.param_groups: g['lr']*=0.5
                lowered=True
        # evaluate final test accuracies for all seen
        for t in self.seen:
            acc = self.eval_task(t, 'test')
            self.hist.setdefault(t, []).append(acc)
            self.best_seen[t] = max(self.best_seen.get(t,0.0), acc)
    def metrics(self):
        last_accs=[self.hist[t][-1] for t in self.seen]
        omega_acc=sum(last_accs)/len(last_accs)
        forg=[max(0.0, self.best_seen[t]-self.hist[t][-1]) for t in self.seen]
        omega_forg=sum(forg)/len(forg)
        return omega_acc, omega_forg
```


Experiment 2: Scaled vision continual-learning benchmark (CIFAR-100 CIL)
Goal
- Demonstrate DyCLOS’ benefit on a standard class-incremental learning (CIL) setup, showing low compute overhead and positive transfer. Larger model and more realistic data dynamics than E1.

Data/Tasks
- CIFAR-100 split into 10 tasks of 10 classes each (class-incremental). Use avalanche.benchmarks.classic.SplitCIFAR100 with 10 experiences.
- Create 5 independent random task permutations; use the same five seeds across baselines for fair comparison.
- Probes: 512 examples per task per seed; sample uniformly per class.
- Robustness stressor: inject a synthetic noisy duplicate task at position 5 (copy of one earlier 10-class subset with random labels) across seeds; included for a subset of runs to test misclassification of similarity.

Model and Training
- Model: ViT-B/16 (timm) pretrained on ImageNet-21k. Replace classifier by a task-specific linear head per task.
- Adaptation: LoRA r=16 on attention qkv/proj, MLP fc1/fc2; IA3 for MLP. Train only adapters + task heads.
- Hyperparameters: 5 epochs per task, batch 256, AdamW lr=1e-4, wd=0.05, cosine LR schedule per task; data transforms: RandomResizedCrop(224), RandAugment(2, 9), Mixup 0.1 (optional, consistent across baselines).
- AMP enabled; gradient accumulation if memory-limited.

DyCLOS specifics
- Window k=4, beam b=8.
- Sdata: Sinkhorn OT (POT) in ViT first-block embeddings for accuracy; cap compute by subsampling embeddings if needed (e.g., 256).
- Sint: cosine of average LoRA+IA3 gradient vectors using 8 micro-batches; projection to 1024 dims.
- α,β tuning: optuna on a held-out micro-stream of 3 tasks (sampled from CIFAR-100 but disjoint classes) for ≤20 trials; objective minimizes Ωforg subject to a small penalty on Ωacc drop. Reuse α,β for all seeds.

Baselines
- Finetune, ER-Reservoir (buffer=2k) with LoRA using avalanche ExperienceReplay, APD/IA3-only (no ordering), MC-SGD (mode connectivity SGD, using existing implementations if available; otherwise omit), LoRA-replay (buffer=2k), Model-Merge (adapter merging via simple averaging), chronological ordering (class index order).

Metrics and Protocol
- Evaluate Ωacc, Ωforg, Transfer-Gain, overhead per seed; average over 5 seeds with 95% CIs.
- Evaluate after each task on all test sets.
- Statistical tests: DyCLOS vs. best fixed-order baseline.

Why this validates
- CIFAR-100 CIL is a community standard; it reveals forgetting without massive memory. DyCLOS should improve final average accuracy and halve forgetting with small overhead.

Key implementation details (E2)
- Use avalanche to create the CIL stream and to implement ER baselines. DyCLOS runs outside avalanche’s scheduler by choosing which next task to train; integrate by mapping DyCLOS’ selected experience order to avalanche experiences.

Example code snippets (E2)

1) CIFAR-100 CIL with avalanche stream and mapping to DyCLOS

2) α,β tuning with optuna (small budget; reuse across seeds)

```python
import optuna

def objective(trial):
    alpha = trial.suggest_float('alpha', 0.1, 3.0, log=True)
    beta  = trial.suggest_float('beta', 0.1, 3.0, log=True)
    # Build a 3-task micro-stream (disjoint from main stream for fairness)
    # Compute DyCLOS order, train adapters quickly (e.g., 1 epoch/task), return Ωforg with Ωacc penalty
    omega_acc, omega_forg = run_microstream(alpha, beta)  # implement using the same trainer
    return omega_forg + 0.1 * max(0.0, 0.8 - omega_acc)  # encourage high acc

study = optuna.create_study(direction='minimize')
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=20, timeout=3600)
alpha_opt, beta_opt = study.best_params['alpha'], study.best_params['beta']
```


Experiment 3: Multi-dataset NLP stream (text classification)
Goal
- Show DyCLOS is modality-agnostic. Validate signals remain informative in language models where datasets vary in label spaces and styles.

Data/Tasks
- 12 tasks: SST-2, IMDB, Yelp Polarity, Amazon Polarity, AG News, DBPedia, TREC-6, Emotion, Banking77, HateXplain (binary), TweetEval-Sentiment, Yahoo Answers (subset).
- Use HuggingFace datasets; unify to text classification format with task-specific heads. Reserve a 512-sample probe per task.
- Use stratified sampling for probes where possible.

Model and Training
- Backbone: roberta-base or deberta-v3-base (transformers).
- Adaptation: LoRA r=16 on attention and FFN; IA3 on FFN. Use peft; task-specific classification head per task.
- Hyperparameters: AdamW lr=2e-5, batch 64, 3 epochs per task, max length=256 tokens; linear warmup 10% of steps per task; weight decay 0.01.
- Mixed precision; bitsandbytes 8-bit weights for base (optional) with 16-bit adapters.

DyCLOS specifics
- Window k=4, beam b=6.
- Sdata: embeddings from tokenizer + first encoder layer (freeze all base weights); pool via mean over sequence or [CLS] token if available.
- Sint: cosine of average adapter gradient vectors using 8 micro-batches; projection to 1024 dims.
- α,β tuning: optuna on a held-out 4-task micro-stream for ≤15 trials (reuse across seeds).

Baselines
- Finetune, ER-Reservoir (buffer=2k) with LoRA, APD/IA3-only, LoRA-replay, Model-Merge, chronological order.

Metrics and Protocol
- Ωacc, Ωforg, Transfer-Gain, overhead; 5 seeds with random task permutations; 95% CIs.
- Extra analysis: monitor per-dataset Transfer-Gain to inspect when DyCLOS induces positive transfer vs. avoidance of interference.

Why this validates
- Confirms genericity of DyCLOS for NLP and shows that probes are inexpensive compared to training. Demonstrates combined signals outperform single-signal ablations.

Reliability enhancements (used across all experiments)
- 5 random seeds per setting; for each seed:
  - Reshuffle task orders (for fixed-order baselines use those permutations without DyCLOS).
  - Independently sample probe subsets.
- Confidence intervals: 95% CIs via bootstrapping over seeds; report per-stream mean ± CI.
- Significance: paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing DyCLOS to best non-DyCLOS baseline for Ωacc and Ωforg; report effect size (Cliff’s delta).
- Ablations: similarity-only (β=0), interference-only (α=0), random ordering (shuffle), window size k ∈ {2,3,4,6}, adapter vs. full fine-tune (single run due to cost) to confirm parameter-efficiency.
- Robustness: noisy task injection (E1 and E2), and perturb probe size (128, 256, 512) to show stable performance and overhead.
- Compute accounting: measure wall-time with and without DyCLOS; log GPU util; separate time spent on probes, sinkhorn, and beam search. Use torch.profiler (optional) to confirm <5% overhead.


Integrated verification and non-overlap across experiments
- E1 focuses on mechanism sanity: shows DyCLOS learns from signals and avoids synthetic interference; includes full ablation suite.
- E2 emphasizes practical scaling on a standard vision CIL benchmark and rigorous overhead accounting; includes noisy task stressor once to avoid overlap.
- E3 demonstrates modality-agnosticism in NLP and verifies that both signals matter in text; avoids repeating E1’s synthetic constructs or E2’s replay-centric analysis.


Compute considerations and scalability
- Mixed precision everywhere; gradient checkpointing in larger backbones; deepspeed ZeRO-3 optional when scaling to ViT-L/14 or LLaMA-1 1.3B.
- Bitsandbytes 8-bit for transformer base weights in NLP, adapters in fp16.
- Probes capped at 512 samples and 8 micro-batches for Sint; projection to 1024 dims ensures Sint compute is cheap.
- α,β BO search amortized cost: constrain trials and reuse across seeds to keep total overhead ≤5%.


Optional scale-up notes (if resources permit)

- Language: LLaMA-1 1.3B via transformers + peft (qlora if memory-limited). Keep the DyCLOS probe unchanged; only adapters train.


What to report (final artifacts)
- For each experiment: Ωacc, Ωforg, Transfer-Gain, Overhead with 95% CIs over 5 seeds.
- Plots: per-task accuracy curves, forgetting per task, chosen DyCLOS order vs. chronological/random with edge costs per transition.

import os

import random
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple, Any, Optional

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader, Subset

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
